title: After
contentNote: This chapter touches on how the war stayed with Henry in later life, including the memories that troubled him when he was old.
summary: In short: Henry came home in December 1918 and married Nell on 28 December. He drove one of Yeovil's first charabancs and later long-distance lorries, kept prize canaries and budgies, and raised three children. He had been gassed, and his breathing was never right again. He never talked about the war, but it stayed with him. He died on 18 January 1963.

scenes.title: Home
scenes.intro: Henry landed at Hull on 4 December 1918. Just over three weeks later, on 28 December, he married Ellen Mary Taylor, known as Nell, at the parish church in Maperton, Somerset.

context.text: Returning prisoners landed at Hull, Leith or Dover, went by train to reception camps such as Ripon, and were given two months' leave, £2 and a printed letter of welcome from the King. Many came home still in prison-camp clothes.

Leaving the army, a man could take a suit of plain clothes or 52 shillings and sixpence, and was insured against being out of work for up to 26 weeks. In the Class Z Reserve he could be recalled "in the event of a grave national emergency".
context.source: The Long, Long Trail, Demobilisation and discharge

context.text: Discharged to the Class Z Reserve on 13 March 1919.

Married at Maperton parish church on 28 December 1918, by licence. Henry, a bachelor, gave his rank as Lance Corporal and his home as Maperton; Nell, a spinster, lived in Yeovil. Both fathers, Arthur Bowles and Henry Taylor, were labourers.

photos.caption: Henry and Nell on their wedding day, 28 December 1918. Henry is still in uniform: he stayed a soldier, on prisoner-of-war leave, until March 1919.
photos.alt: Henry in army uniform and peaked cap, with a moustache, standing beside Nell in a wide-brimmed hat and dark coat.

photos.caption: Henry and Nell's marriage certificate, 28 December 1918. He gave his rank as "Soldier, L. Corp": a Lance Corporal, still in the army just over three weeks after landing back in England.
photos.alt: A green-bordered handwritten certificate headed Certified Copy of an Entry of Marriage, with a red one-penny King George V stamp at the foot. A full transcript follows.
transcript: The Parish Church, in the Parish of Maperton, in the County of Somerset. Entry number 105
Henry John Bowles, aged 25, bachelor. Rank or profession: Soldier, L. Corp. Residence: Maperton
Ellen Mary Taylor, aged 25, spinster. Residence: Yeovil
According to the rites and ceremonies of the Church of England, by licence
Harry Taylor and Ethel Joyce Bowles (the handwriting of both names is hard to read)
Cyril White, Rector of Maperton, 28th December 1918
photos.transcriptNote: The register gives Henry's age as 25. By his birth certificate he was 24, six months short of 25. Small slips like this were common.

photos.caption: About 1919 to 1920: Henry and Nell, seated, with baby Gilbert. Behind Henry stand his parents, Arthur Bowles and his wife; behind Nell, her brother George Taylor; on the right, Nell's parents, Mr and Mrs Taylor.
photos.alt: A sepia family group in a garden: a young man and a young woman holding a baby in a long white gown sit in front of two older couples and a younger man.

photos.caption: The King's letter to returning prisoners: "The Queen joins me in welcoming you". Does the family still have Henry's?
photos.alt: A framed printed letter with a royal crest.

paras: Home. Mother didn't say anything at all, just held on to me in the doorway till Father said let the boy in, he's letting the cold in. Then she cried, and then she made tea, the way she did the day I told her I'd joined.
The little ones aren't little. Some of them are taller than me now. They look at me like they're waiting for me to say something about it. I don't.
They've given us two months' leave, two pounds, and a letter from the King. I've put the King's letter in the drawer.
And I'm to be married. Nell and me, this month. I can hardly believe it's me writing that, in this same book. The same pencil, near enough. A month ago I was behind wire in Germany.
I'll be a married man for Christmas.
basis: Landed at Hull on 4 December 1918 (casualty record).
He married Ellen Mary Taylor on 28 December 1918 at Maperton parish church, giving his home as Maperton and his rank as Lance Corporal (their marriage certificate).
Returning prisoners were given two months' leave, a £2 payment and a printed letter of welcome from King George V (Great War Forum accounts).
His parents, Arthur Bowles and his wife, both lived into their nineties (Grandma Angela's memoir).

paras: Finished with the Army. Class Z Reserve, they call it, which means they can have me back if there's another war, and God help us if there is.

Back on the land. The work's the same as it ever was, the horses and the plough and the weather, and it's a comfort, it's the only comfort some days. A furrow either runs straight or it doesn't. Nobody gets killed if it doesn't.
I don't sleep so well. Nell says I talk in the night. I tell her it's nothing. The cold gets on my chest too, since the gas, and some mornings I'm coughing before I'm out of bed.

This is the last page in this book I'm going to write. It's done its job. I'll put it away with the King's letter and the medals when they come, and I'll not talk about any of it, not to anybody. Some things you carry so the others don't have to.
God bless them all. Ours and theirs.
basis: Discharged to the Class Z Army Reserve on 13 March 1919 (casualty record).
Class Z men went back to civilian life but could be recalled "in the event of a grave national emergency" (The Long, Long Trail).

He was a farm hand after the war; a photograph is described of him with baby Gilbert on a plough behind a horse. He "never talked to anybody about the War", and late in life he was troubled by memories of it (Grandma Angela's memoir).
"Grandad had been gassed during WWI in France and since then had always had problems breathing" (Memories of Grandad). When and where is not recorded.
The notebook itself is imagined, and so is everything Henry says here.

scenes.title: The farm and the lorries
scenes.intro: Henry and Nell had three children: Gilbert Henry Arthur, Joyce, always called Joycie, born on 22 July 1921, and William George, known as Bill, born in 1924. These memories are their granddaughter Angela's, with some from Joyce's grandson Tristan.

stories.title: On the mower
stories.body: Grandma Angela's memoir remembers a photograph of Henry on a plough with baby Gilbert on his lap. Here it is. In fact it shows a horse-drawn grass mower, with two heavy horses in harness. Where and when it was taken is not known.
stories.source: Grandma Angela's memoir, page 1

stories.title: The charabanc
stories.body: He drove for the rest of his working life, and never took a driving test. Later he became a long-distance lorry driver.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: one of the first men in Yeovil to drive a Charabanc
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Bird Brothers and British Road Services
stories.body: In 1924 the family moved to 67 Southville, Yeovil, the year their youngest, Bill, was born. Henry drove for Bird Brothers, and later long-distance lorries for British Road Services. The 1939 Register lists him at 67 Southville as a lorry driver, "heavy worker".
stories.source: Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: Twelve miles an hour
stories.body: In 1924 two policemen timed his lorry over a measured furlong near Blandford: 16 miles 928 yards an hour, when the limit for a heavy lorry was 12. Henry said he was sorry, and told the constable that lorries ought to be made to carry speedometers. He was fined ten shillings. In 1935 he was fined £1 for going over 20 miles an hour.
stories.source: Newspaper reports, from Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: A working man
stories.body: In 1931 a policeman at Broadwindsor stopped his lorry, carrying the sections of a building laid flat, 9 feet wide, too wide to pass another lorry. Henry wrote to the magistrates pleading guilty. He had not meant it, he said, and hoped they would be lenient. The case was dismissed with a caution.
stories.source: Newspaper report, 17 July 1931, from Tristan Cobb's family research
stories.quote: only a working man with a wife and three children

stories.title: Knight of the Road
stories.body: For all that, he was given a "Knight of the Road" award for his driving, and he had never taken a driving test.
stories.source: Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: "Hello then"
stories.body: On holiday in a hired car, if another driver did something wrong, Henry wound down the window and said "hello then". Asked if he knew them, he said: "No, but they know what I mean."
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Half a crown
stories.body: When Joyce was home on leave from the ATS, he bet her half a crown that she couldn't reverse his lorry and trailer into a space. "And he had to pay up as she did it perfectly."
stories.source: Grandma Angela's memoir, page 1

stories.title: Pack it away
stories.body: The story goes, from Joyce, that if she or her brothers came home and left anything lying about, like shoes kicked off after a dance, Henry would go and wake them up and tell them to put it away: their mother was not their servant.
stories.source: Joyce Bush's memory, from Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: Burnt to a crisp
stories.body: It is said he liked his bacon burnt to a crisp, just as his great-grandson Tristan does.
stories.source: Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: The bird hospital
stories.body: He turned an old shed into an aviary for canaries and budgies, with two cages kept for sick birds: his "bird hospital". Seed and water were measured out exactly. He showed his birds in Yeovil and usually came home with certificates. He was a member of the cage bird association in Yeovil, and built the aviary in his back garden.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright; Tristan Cobb's family research
stories.quote: It was special to do that with him.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: The Bowles day out
stories.body: Twice the whole family hired two coaches for a day out, once to Badbury Rings near Wimborne: all twelve brothers and sisters, their husbands and wives, children and grandchildren, with crates of beer in the boot. Henry hardly relaxed all day. He was worried how his brothers would behave after a drink. He enjoyed a beer or cider himself, but "would never get drunk".
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: The Buffaloes
stories.body: He was a member of the Royal Antediluvian Order of Buffaloes, and head of the lodge opposite the Salvation Army in Southville, Yeovil. He won many Buffaloes medals, which are now kept by his granddaughter Angela.
stories.source: Grandma Angela's memoir, page 1; Tristan Cobb's family research

photos.caption: Henry with little Gilbert on his lap, on a horse-drawn mower behind two heavy horses, about 1920.
photos.alt: Two large dark working horses in harness pull a mowing machine through long grass; a man in a hat and waistcoat sits on the seat holding a small child in white.

photos.caption: The three children, about 1930. From the left: Bill, the youngest, Joyce and Gilbert.
photos.alt: A studio photograph of two boys in jackets and long socks either side of a girl in a pale dress.

photos.caption: Henry and Nell with their grown-up children, before the children went off to the Second World War. Standing, from the left: Bill, Joyce and Gilbert.
photos.alt: A studio portrait of an older couple seated, the woman in round glasses, with two young men in suits and a young woman in pearls standing behind them.

photos.caption: Henry's medals from the Royal Antediluvian Order of Buffaloes, now kept by his granddaughter Angela. Some carry the names of lodge offices, such as Minstrel, Waiter and Primo.
photos.alt: Seventeen medals laid out in three rows on a table, each hanging from a striped ribbon with an ornate bar. The medals are crosses, stars and round badges, one with a buffalo's head; a long sash with a round badge lies at the end of the bottom row.
photos.credit: Family photograph, from Tristan Cobb's family research

photos.caption: Henry, crouching on the left, beside his British Road Services lorry, NLJ 958, after a crash. The front of the cab is smashed. When and where it happened is not known.
photos.alt: A badly damaged lorry with a crushed cab and broken windscreen, its front wheels in a grassy ditch. The registration plate reads NLJ 958. A man in a cap crouches at the bottom left, beside the front of the lorry.
photos.credit: Family photograph, from Tristan Cobb's family research
photos.with: Bird Brothers and British Road Services

photos.caption: Grandad and Angela with one of his birds, in the 1950s. He kept canaries and budgies, and showed them in Yeovil.
photos.alt: A man in a sleeveless pullover kneels in a vegetable garden beside a small girl. Together they hold a bird cage standing on a wooden stool, with a terrace of houses behind them.
photos.credit: Family photograph, lent by Angela Wright

scenes.title: Grandad
scenes.intro: When her father was called up by the Navy for the Korean War and her mother went back to work, his granddaughter spent her days at Henry and Nell's house in Southville. "Those were just lovely days."

stories.title: Flat cap and boots
stories.body: Outdoors he always wore a flat cap, boots and a belt, with his sleeves rolled up in summer. On the beach at Weymouth he sat in a deckchair in shoes, socks, long trousers, shirt and cap. Just occasionally he took off his shoes and socks, rolled up his trousers and paddled.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: I can't even remember him in trunks or going for a swim.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: The hand and the belt
stories.body: He was a strong disciplinarian. "Grandad would tell me that I would have his belt. That Never happened. Just a movement of hand was all that was needed."
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: Grandad never showed anything but love.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Queen and princess
stories.body: She spent almost fourteen years growing up with him in her life.
stories.source: Grandma Angela's memoir, page 1
stories.quote: I was always Grandad's queen and when Sandra came along she was his princess.

stories.title: Report day
stories.body: Henry and Nell lived halfway between school and home, so on school report day she would pop in and persuade them to open her report first, "so I would know what the marks were before I got home. Very helpful at times."
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

photos.caption: Henry and Nell walking arm in arm in Weymouth, Henry in his flat cap.
photos.alt: An older couple walk towards the camera along a seaside promenade with flags behind them. The man wears a flat cap, jacket and pullover; the woman, in round glasses, wears a long coat over a pale dress.
photos.credit: Family photograph, from Tristan Cobb's family research

photos.caption: Grandma, Grandad and Angela on the beach at Weymouth, in the early 1950s. Henry is in shirt, braces and long trousers, just as Angela remembers him at the seaside.
photos.alt: On a crowded beach, an older woman in round glasses and a flowered dress and a man in an open-necked shirt and braces sit in deckchairs either side of a small fair-haired girl with a bow in her hair. Beach huts and seafront buildings are behind them.
photos.credit: Family photograph, lent by Angela Wright

photos.caption: At Aunty Winnie's bungalow in Poole, in the 1950s. Standing, from the left: Grandad, Grandma Bush (Angela's other grandmother) and Grandma Nell. Kneeling: Aunty Winnie, Henry's sister, and Angela.
photos.alt: Five people outside a pebble-dashed bungalow. Standing are a man in shirt and braces, a very elderly woman in a dark dress holding a walking stick, and a woman in round glasses and a flowered dress. Kneeling in front are a smiling woman in a flowered dress and a young girl in a checked dress with a white collar.
photos.credit: Family photograph, lent by Angela Wright

photos.caption: Grandad and Angela on the grass at the Nothe, Weymouth, in about 1962, when she was 13. His cap lies on the grass beside him.
photos.alt: A white-haired man in a shirt with rolled sleeves and dark trousers sits on a grassy slope beside a teenage girl in a sun hat, blouse and full skirt. A pale cap and a dark jacket lie on the grass beside him.
photos.credit: Family photograph, lent by Angela Wright

scenes.title: Nell
scenes.intro: In his granddaughter's memory, Henry and Nell came "as a package". Nell deserves her own page.

stories.title: In service
stories.body: Before she married, Nell had been in service. She made sure her granddaughter learned to lay a table properly, every day, not just on special occasions.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: I still try to do that today.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: The motorbike
stories.body: Nell sat on a backless chair by the sink to do the vegetables. Her granddaughter sat behind with her arms round her waist, and it became their motorbike, taking sharp corners and racing to the crossroads.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: Things you do for your granddaughter.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: The Army
stories.body: Nell went to the Salvation Army, and took her granddaughter to the Sunday meetings, to the Corps on holiday in Weymouth, and to her midweek ladies' services. On Saturdays it might be fish and chips at Thorpes, with bread and butter, and grace before they ate.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: It was Grandma that taught me about Jesus and how to trust Him.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Sunday dinner
stories.body: Sunday lunches were a family time, with Uncle Bill, who lived with them. Nell was a good cook.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: The only time
stories.body: Nell died of cancer on 5 June 1961, aged 67. That morning, her granddaughter called in as usual. Henry was alone in the garden.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright; Tristan Cobb's family research
stories.quote: As I walked down the path I could see he was crying. That was the only time I saw him cry.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

scenes.title: What he carried
scenes.intro: Henry never talked about the war. But it never quite left him.

stories.title: The silence
stories.body: Like many men of his generation, he kept the war to himself.
stories.source: Grandma Angela's memoir, page 10
stories.quote: A part that he didn't talk about, because I think it was too raw for him to do so.

stories.title: What the family knew
stories.body: The stories of him in the Great War were few. The family knew he had been a prisoner, and that he brought the walking stick home. Joyce's husband, Cyril Bush, always believed Henry had served in the Somerset Light Infantry. Nobody mentioned the Wiltshire Regiment, where he spent most of his war. He did tell them he had been gassed, which is why they went to Weymouth for the sea air.
stories.source: Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: Gassed
stories.body: Every winter he had bronchitis and chest infections. His army record doesn't mention gas, so we don't know when it happened. His Wiltshire battalion met mustard gas near Ypres in July 1917, though Henry may only have rejoined it that August. When he died in 1963, his death certificate gave acute and chronic bronchitis as the cause.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright; his death certificate
stories.quote: Grandad had been gassed during WWI in France and since then had always had problems breathing.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Weymouth
stories.body: The sea air and the flat Promenade at Weymouth were good for his chest, so for years the family took their holidays there, in a flat on the Nothe side of the harbour, with their neighbours from Southville. Fishermen gave them spare fish.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: On days when grandad couldn't walk too far he would have a chair on the harbour and enjoyed chatting to those passing by.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: The barbed wire
stories.body: Towards the end of his life he grew less tolerant; her piano lessons lasted two weeks, because he couldn't stand the noise. And he began to see things that weren't there.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: Asking me to get the barbed wire off him and stop people running all over him.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Understanding
stories.body: She only understood what he had been living through many years later, when she read Sebastian Faulks's novel Birdsong.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: At the time I had no idea what he meant or wanted.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: What we know now
stories.body: Doctors in Henry's time called it shell shock. Today we would recognise much of it as post-traumatic stress: a real injury to the mind, which can return in old age. Many veterans of both world wars were troubled by memories late in life.
stories.source: Science Museum, Wounded: from shell shock to PTSD

asks.q: What was a gas attack like?
What were the mines, and who dug them?

paras: Bad night again. My chest like a sack of wet sand, and the dreams.
It's always the wire. I'm caught on it and I can't get free, and they're coming over, all of them, running, and nobody sees me. I wake up and Bill's in the doorway saying Dad, Dad, it's all right.
The little one was here today practising her piano, and I couldn't bear it, God forgive me. Every note went right through me. I told her mother it was the noise. It wasn't the noise.
Forty-odd years and I never told a soul. I thought if I kept it shut away it would stay there. It doesn't stay. It waits.
Still. I've had a good life, better than most of them got. The garden, the birds, the grandchildren running in and out. That's what it was for. That's what it was all for.
basis: Late in life he asked his granddaughter to "get the barbed wire off him and stop people running all over him". Her piano lessons at his house lasted two weeks because he couldn't stand the noise. He was gassed, and had breathing problems for the rest of his life. His son Bill lived with him (Memories of Grandad).
He never talked about the war: "it was too raw for him" (Grandma Angela's memoir).
Every word. These are thoughts written for Henry, not things he said. He never told anyone.

scenes.title: A happy note
scenes.intro: Henry died at Yeovil General Hospital on 18 January 1963, aged 68. His granddaughter Angela was two days short of her fourteenth birthday.

stories.title: A happy note
stories.body: Henry and Nell had 3 children, 4 grandchildren and 10 great-grandchildren, and when Grandma Angela wrote her memoir there were 10 great-great-grandchildren, and counting.
stories.source: Grandma Angela's memoir, page 10
stories.quote: Grandad's life did end on a happy note

stories.title: Together again
stories.body: Henry was buried with Nell at Yeovil Cemetery, in grave B3817. In March 1963 his affairs were settled by Joyce and Bill, then a confectionery salesman. He left £382 4s.
stories.source: Probate calendar and burial record, from Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: Their sons
stories.body: Henry and Nell outlived one of their sons. Gilbert died of peritonitis on 21 January 1948, and never saw his own son, John. Bill never married, lived with his parents, and died on 28 January 1968.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Thank you
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: Grandma and Grandad, you were such a wonderful example to me. Thank you.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

photos.caption: Henry's death certificate, January 1963. The cause of death, bronchitis and heart failure, is the chest trouble the family always linked to his being gassed in the war. The copy was issued to his daughter, Joyce Bush.
photos.alt: A printed form headed Certified Copy of an Entry of Death, with typed entries in columns. A full transcript follows.

photos.caption: Henry and Nell, at a relative's bungalow in Portishead. The last photograph taken before Nell died.
photos.alt: An elderly woman with white hair and glasses leaning out of an open window, smiling, and an elderly man in a jumper sitting outside below her, also smiling.

photos.caption: Joyce's wedding, 13 September 1947, with Henry and Nell on the right.
photos.alt: A wedding group of six: the bride holding a large bouquet beside the groom, with the parents of the couple and the best man.
